<reason>Both sides built sophisticated, well-grounded cases. B's opening ratchet theory and its Rebuttal 1 point that disclosed discounts (student/senior) survive only because of verification gates that algorithmic personalization lacks was the single sharpest rebuttal of the debate, genuinely damaging A's central counter-example and exposing that A's own midnight-plumber illustration fell outside A's proposed buyer-identity/sale-conditions line. However, A adapted with a workable enforcement proposal (the swap test plus aggregate disclosure/right-to-ask), kept the scope disciplined throughout, and in the pressure round extracted a real concession from B (that the unsophisticated already pay the most and disclosure won't lift them), which A's closing used effectively to reframe B as defending a harmful status quo rather than a genuine welfare-enhancing mechanism. Crucially, A's proxy-discrimination and market-signal-corrosion arguments from the opening were never squarely answered by B, leaving a live, unrebutted route for A. B's closing mirrored A's rhetoric well but mostly repeated the arms-race point rather than resolving the discrimination-oversight line or fully defusing A's fork. A's Rebuttal 1 being clipped is a real execution cost, but the lost material was a closing flourish rather than load-bearing content. On balance A ends the debate with the cleaner, more complete path to the resolution as written.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 1 point that student/senior discounts survive disclosure only because of verification gates, which algorithmic personalization lacks, directly undercutting A's chosen counter-example — countered only partially by A's later swap-test/aggregate-disclosure proposal in Rebuttal 2.</best_rebuttal>
